hook: For 1,000 monthly $20 subscriptions, the modeled fees are $1,120 on Stripe with no-code Tax, $1,520 with Tax API, $1,600 on Lemon Squeezy and $1,500 on Paddle. The integration path and subscription surcharge change the ranking.

sections.title: Start with a defined account and checkout
sections.content:
These are standard US Stripe card rates, not a quote for a Korean business. Eligibility, negotiated contracts, tax treatment and settlement currency must be checked before choosing a provider.

| Stripe component | Published rate | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Domestic cards | 2.9% + 30¢ | successful charge |
| International cards | +1.5% | applicable international cards |
| Currency conversion | +1% | when conversion is required |
| Billing pay-as-you-go | 0.7% | Billing volume |
| Tax Basic no-code | 0.5% | registered transactions |
| Tax Basic API | 50¢ | registered transactions |

No-code Tax applies to integrations such as Checkout and Billing. The API price is a different integration path, not a fee to add to the no-code rate. Registration, filing and optional services need their own budget.

sections.title: The two merchants have different fee rules
sections.content:
Lemon Squeezy and Paddle advertise a base 5% + 50¢, but that does not make their subscription invoices identical.

- Lemon Squeezy adds 0.5 percentage points for subscriptions, 1.5 for applicable non-US transactions and 1.5 for PayPal. Its fee uses the total order value, including tax.
- Paddle advertises 5% + 50¢ per Checkout transaction with subscriptions included. Do not copy Lemon Squeezy surcharges onto Paddle.
- Account-specific pricing, payouts and optional services can change either result.

A merchant of record handles covered transaction tax obligations as the seller. That is not a promise that your business has no income-tax, reporting or other legal obligations. Compare the service scope as well as the checkout fee.

sections.title: Four invoices for the same subscription volume
sections.content:
Assume 1,000 successful $20 renewals: $20,000 charged, no added tax, refunds, disputes, FX or payout fees. Use US domestic cards for Stripe and no international or PayPal surcharge for Lemon Squeezy; assume every transaction incurs the chosen Tax Basic fee.

| Provider / path | Arithmetic | Total |
|---|---|---|
| Stripe + no-code Tax | $580 + $300 Payments + $140 Billing + $100 Tax | $1,120 |
| Stripe + Tax API | $580 + $300 + $140 + $500 | $1,520 |
| Lemon Squeezy subscription | 5.5% × $20,000 + 1,000 × $0.50 | $1,600 |
| Paddle standard | 5% × $20,000 + 1,000 × $0.50 | $1,500 |

Correction, November 14: the earlier $1,500 Lemon Squeezy subscription example omitted its surcharge. The old universal $21.43 crossover also assumed the Tax API path and Paddle's base rate, not every subscription setup.

sections.title: Country and tax change the denominator
sections.content:
Use the actual checkout total, not just the advertised product price. A hypothetical $20 subscription with 20% tax creates a $24 order; if Lemon Squeezy's non-US surcharge applies, its fee is 7% × $24 + $0.50 = $2.18, before payout costs.

| Change from the base model | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Lemon Squeezy non-US subscription | 7% + 50¢; PayPal can add another 1.5 points |
| Stripe international card | add 1.5 points to its applicable stack |
| Stripe FX conversion | add 1 point when required |
| Tax-inclusive versus tax-exclusive price | calculate from the actual fee base |

Lemon Squeezy also documents region-dependent payout fees. These are separate from checkout fees and excluded from the worked totals. Paddle's own contract and payout terms must be evaluated separately; a foreign buyer alone does not establish which provider wins.

sections.title: The crossover belongs to one set of assumptions
sections.content:
With the same tax-free US model, Stripe plus no-code Tax is 4.1% × P + $0.30 per charge, lower than both modeled MoR fees at every positive P. With Tax API it is 3.6% × P + $0.80.

- Against Paddle: $0.30 / (5% − 3.6%) = $21.43.
- Against a Lemon Squeezy subscription: $0.30 / (5.5% − 3.6%) = $15.79.
- A $9 Lemon Squeezy subscription costs $0.995 before other fees, not the $0.95 base one-time illustration.

Those are processing comparisons, not total operating costs. Neither result prices engineering, tax registration, filing, buyer support or risk. A cheaper fee model can still be the more expensive business process.

sections.title: Choose the service before trusting the headline
sections.content:
For Stripe Payments with Billing, you remain the seller. Tax Basic is calculation and collection tooling; Tax Complete offers a separate registration and filing service with its own plans and limits. Stripe also markets Managed Payments as a distinct MoR product, which is outside these calculations.

For a covered Paddle or Lemon Squeezy sale, the provider is the merchant of record. Approval, product eligibility, refunds, chargebacks, payout timing and reserves still matter.

- Confirm the business and bank country are supported.
- Obtain the applicable rate card and test a representative receipt.
- Model the real card mix, tax totals and average charge.
- Check migration and data portability with both providers before committing.

A checkout demo is not proof of live eligibility or settlement. None of the examples establishes that a Korean account will be approved or receive the modeled net amount.

verdict_summary: There is no single merchant-of-record invoice. In the defined $20 subscription model, Stripe no-code Tax costs $1,120, Stripe Tax API $1,520, Lemon Squeezy $1,600 and Paddle $1,500. Choose using the actual integration, country, tax base and service scope, not the shared 5% headline.
migration_guide: Ask both providers to confirm supported subscription and payment-data migration, required customer consent, settlement reconciliation and historical tax-record handling before scheduling a move. Do not assume either automatic portability or that every customer must re-enter a card. Run a small approved migration test before moving active renewals; retaining access to old records does not transfer earlier obligations.

faqs.q: Is 5% + 50¢ the full subscription fee on both MoRs?
faqs.a: No. Lemon Squeezy adds 0.5 percentage points for subscriptions and may add international and PayPal fees. Paddle advertises subscriptions within its standard 5% + 50¢ rate. Check each account contract and payout costs separately.

faqs.q: Does Stripe Tax always cost 50¢ per transaction?
faqs.a: No. The US Tax Basic page distinguishes 0.5% no-code integrations from a 50¢ API integration charge for applicable registered transactions. They are alternative paths, not two fees to add together.

faqs.q: What changes the international comparison?
faqs.a: Stripe lists +1.5% for international cards and +1% when currency conversion is required. Lemon Squeezy lists +1.5% for applicable non-US transactions and +1.5% for PayPal. Tax-inclusive order totals and payout costs also matter.

faqs.q: Do these calculations prove Korean eligibility or remove all tax duties?
faqs.a: No. Verify supported business and bank countries, account approval, settlement and legal obligations. MoR transaction-tax handling is not a blanket exemption from the seller business’s own taxes or reporting.

hook: Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol list the same standard rate: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output. Equal rates do not establish equal costs for the same documents. Count each model separately; there is no measured Claude-versus-GPT token ratio established here.

sections.title: Two sheets, one identical sticker
sections.content:
The flagship rows of both price sheets match to the cent, and so do the cache reads.

| Per million tokens | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|
| Input | $2.00 | $2.00 |
| Output | $10.00 | $10.00 |
| Cached input (hit) | $0.10 | $0.10 |
| 5m or 30m cache write | $2.50 (1.25x) | $2.50 (1.25x) |
| Batch input / output | $1.00 / $5.00 | $1.00 / $5.00 |

Anthropic's Opus 5.5 sits one rung up at $4 and $20, with cache reads at $0.20. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra sits at $10 and $50. On the flagship row there is nothing to choose, which is the first sign that the model price is not the decision.

sections.title: The tokenizer note is not a cross-vendor benchmark
sections.content:
Anthropic describes a tokenizer change between newer and earlier Claude models, not between Claude and GPT. Its approximate 30% increase depends on the text and workload. That note cannot establish a fixed Claude-versus-OpenAI price premium.

There is no universal source-token unit shared by the two vendors. Count the same representative input with each target model, then record actual output usage separately. Generated answers may differ in length, reasoning usage and quality; an input-token ratio does not predict output tokens.

The $1,844 example below assumes equal billed token counts in each category. It is arithmetic, not a measured identical-text benchmark. The separate input-only sensitivity case deliberately leaves the $500 output line unchanged and is not a prediction for either vendor.

Correction, 13 November 2026: removed the unsupported cross-vendor 30% claim and the whole-bill multiplier. Cache controls, hit rates and reuse arithmetic were also corrected on this date; other rates retain their original verification date.

sections.title: Caching is a break-even test, not a discount
sections.content:
For standard short-context Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, the hit rate is $0.10 / $2.00 = 0.05x; other models differ.

| Cache operation | Sonnet 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|
| Short write | 1.25x, 5m | 1.25x, 30m |
| Long write | 2x, 1h | 2.5x, 12h |
| Hit | 0.05x | 0.05x |

Let n be total requests, including the cold first request. One write and n-1 successful full-prefix reads cost w + r(n-1), not w + rn. This excludes fresh input and output and assumes no intervening expiry, prefix change or rewrite.

Short writes: 1.25 + 0.05(n-1) < n means n > 1.2632. At ten requests, 1.25 + 0.05 × 9 = 1.70 versus 10 uncached: 83% less for this prefix alone. With a 0.1x model the corresponding total is 2.15, a 78.5% reduction.

Long writes at 0.05x reads need three total requests (one write, two hits): Sonnet costs 2.10 and Sol costs 2.60 versus 3 uncached. Never count an expired entry as a hit.

sections.title: Batch is the one line where both sheets agree
sections.content:
Both vendors halve input and output for asynchronous work. Anthropic publishes the batch rows separately; OpenAI prints a Batch table and a separate Flex table at the same numbers.

| Batch, per million | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Claude Opus 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | $1.00 | $2.00 | $1.00 |
| Output | $5.00 | $10.00 | $5.00 |

Anthropic's page says its cache multipliers stack with the batch discount. For Sonnet 5.5, apply the 0.05x hit multiplier to the applicable batch input rate only for an actual cache hit; a batch does not guarantee reuse. The trap is that a nightly single-run job has nothing to read from, and a cold cache write just adds 25% to a batch you could have submitted uncached.

sections.title: Long prompts are where the sheets stop being comparable
sections.content:
Both vendors reprice the prompt once it gets long, and they do it in different shapes.

| Prompt size | GPT-6.1 Sol | Claude Haiku 5.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Short context, input | $2.00 | $0.10 up to 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, input | $4.00 | $0.50 over 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, output | $15.00 | $2.50 over 100,000 tokens |

OpenAI's long-context row doubles input and multiplies output by 1.5. Anthropic's Haiku sheet lists two rows, one for prompts up to 100,000 tokens and one for prompts over it, at five times the rate, and it does not print a marginal split.

A 200,000-token prompt therefore bills at 0.2 × $0.50 = $0.10 on the over-100k row against $0.02 if the same prompt fit under the line. That cliff, not the per-token sticker, is what a document pipeline hits when someone pastes a whole contract set.

sections.title: Three add-ons that quietly change the unit
sections.content:
Fast mode on both sides doubles the sticker: Opus 5.5 goes to $8 input and $40 output, GPT-6.1 Sol to $4 and $20. Anthropic notes that fast mode is not available with the Batch API, so the two savings cannot be stacked.

Data residency is a multiplier rather than a tier. Sending Claude 4.6 or later to US-only inference applies 1.1x to every token category, cache writes and reads included.

For exactly two requests 12 hours apart, with no intervening reuse: Anthropic's 1-hour entry has expired: two cold writes cost 2 + 2 = 4 prefix units, not 2 + a cache read. 

For GPT-6.1 Sol, a successful 12-hour-cache hit would cost 2.5 + 0.05 = 2.55 across the pair; two cold writes cost 5. Both exceed two uncached passes at 2. 

This is not a long-run forecast: measure hits, writes and refreshes before extrapolating.

verdict_summary: The named standard rows match: $2 input, $10 output and $0.10 cached input per million tokens. That does not make the same task equally expensive. Measure token usage, output quality, cache hits and retries on a representative sample. Apply the selected model, context and service-tier rates to those measurements; do not multiply a vendor bill by an assumed tokenizer premium.
migration_guide:
Caching controls are not interchangeable. Anthropic Messages is opt-in: top-level cache_control selects an automatic moving breakpoint; block-level cache_control selects explicit breakpoints. GPT-6.1 Sol supports implicit caching and explicit-only breakpoints. Re-measure token usage on migration, rather than transferring an assumed token ratio.

The worked bill uses explicit boundaries around the stable prefix, leaving fresh input outside the write. Batch jobs, files and model-specific configuration also need review when switching providers.

faqs.q: Is prompt caching automatic on both?
faqs.a: Anthropic Messages requires opt-in: use top-level cache_control for automatic breakpoint placement, or block-level cache_control for explicit boundaries. GPT-6.1 Sol supports implicit caching by default and explicit-only controls. Automatic placement does not guarantee a hit.

faqs.q: Do the batch discount and the cache discount combine?
faqs.a: On Anthropic the page says cache multipliers stack with the batch discount. OpenAI publishes separate Batch and Flex tables at the same rates, and fast mode is excluded from batch on Anthropic.

faqs.q: Does the 30% tokenizer note mean Claude costs 30% more than GPT?
faqs.a: No. Anthropic compares newer and earlier Claude tokenizers, not Claude with GPT. The difference depends on content. Measure each target model on the same input and account for generated output separately; this article provides no measured cross-vendor ratio.

faqs.q: Is a cache write ever a loss?
faqs.a: Yes. For Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, count one cold write plus n-1 hits across n requests, with a 0.05x hit rate. Short writes need two total requests; long writes need three. Expiry or changed prefixes add writes, not discounted reads.

hook: Twenty hosts and 5,000 custom series bill $450 a month on Datadog and $19 on Grafana Cloud's Pro plan. The difference is not the per-series rate. It is that only one of them puts the hosts on the invoice.

sections.title: One sells a host, the other sells a series
sections.content:
Datadog's infrastructure line is a licence: $15 per host per month billed annually, $18 month-to-month, and every licence carries 100 custom metrics. Grafana Cloud's Pro plan is a $19 platform fee for the whole account, with 10,000 active series and 50 GB of logs inside it.

That is the whole philosophical difference, and it decides the invoice shape:

- **Datadog:** cost grows with machines first, then with the cardinality of what you send from them.
- **Grafana Cloud:** cost is flat until you pass the account-level allowances, then grows with data volume only.

Neither page hides this. It is written in the billing unit, which is the one line worth reading before the price.

sections.title: The custom metrics line is the one that grows without a deploy
sections.content:
Per unit, Datadog's custom metrics cost $5 per 100 per month, which is $50 per 1,000. Grafana Cloud's first paid band is $6.50 per 1,000, then $5.90 above 100,000 and $5.50 above 200,000.

| Meter | Datadog Infrastructure Pro | Grafana Cloud Pro |
|---|---|---|
| Base | $15 per host per month, annual | $19 per account per month |
| Included series | 100 per host | 10,000 per account |
| Series beyond that | $5 per 100 | $6.50 per 1,000 |
| Effective per 1,000 | $50.00 | $6.50 |

Datadog's rate is 7.7 times Grafana's, and the allotment it ships with is 100 times smaller. Those two numbers pull in opposite directions, so the bill depends on whether your cardinality scales with hosts or with users.

sections.title: Two shops, and the same four numbers
sections.content:
Shop one: 20 hosts, 5,000 custom series.

| Line | Datadog | Grafana Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Platform or hosts | 20 × $15 = $300 | $19 |
| Billable series | 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000 | 0 (5,000 under 10,000) |
| Series cost | 30 × $5 = $150 | $0 |
| **Total** | **$450** | **$19** |

Shop two: 20 hosts, 200,000 custom series, which is what a `user_id` tag does to a counter.

| Line | Datadog | Grafana Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Platform or hosts | $300 | $19 |
| Billable series | 198,000 | 190,000 |
| Series cost | 1,980 × $5 = $9,900 | 90,000 × $6.50/1k + 100,000 × $5.90/1k = $1,175 |
| **Total** | **$10,200** | **$1,194** |

The second table is the one that arrives without a deploy, a migration or a new service. It arrives the week someone adds a tag.

sections.title: Logs: one vendor counts bytes, the other counts events
sections.content:
This is where the two sheets stop being directly comparable. Datadog charges $0.10 per ingested GB, then $1.70 per million indexed events at 15-day retention or $2.50 at 30-day. Grafana charges three meters per GB: $0.05 to process, $0.40 to write and $0.10 to retain, with 50 GB included.

Take 500 GB a month at roughly 2.5 KB per event, or 200 million events, indexed for 30 days.

| Meter | Datadog | Grafana Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest | 500 GB × $0.10 = $50 | 450 GB × $0.05 = $22.50 |
| Index and retain | 200M × $2.50/M = $500 | 450 GB × $0.40 = $180 |
| Retention | included in the index rate | 450 GB × $0.10 = $45 |
| **Total** | **$550** | **$247.50** |

The event meter rewards fat logs and the byte meter rewards few of them. The same 500 GB is $550 or $247.50 depending on which unit your logging happens to satisfy.

sections.title: Both vendors now discount you for deleting tags
sections.content:
Datadog sells Metrics without Limits, which splits one number into two: ingested custom metrics at $0.10 per 100, and indexed ones at $5 per 100. Grafana ships Adaptive Metrics, which aggregates and drops unused series, and the page states the claim as the vendor's own: up to 80%.

Read that as an admission. When a vendor builds a product whose only job is to delete time series before they reach the meter, the meter is cardinality, and the vendor knows the cardinality is often junk.

The practical move costs nothing:

1. Sort your metrics by tag value count, not by metric name.
2. Drop any tag whose values scale with users, carts or request ids.
3. Re-count before you negotiate a discount, because the discount is priced on the number you can already fix.

sections.title: What the switch actually costs
sections.content:
Correction, November 14, 2026: a standard Prometheus client exposes metrics for scraping; it does not directly send to a remote_write endpoint. Pricing figures retain their November 10 check and were not re-quoted in this technical correction.

Typical metrics path: application /metrics → Prometheus scrape + remote_write → Grafana Cloud Metrics. With Alloy: application /metrics → prometheus.scrape → prometheus.remote_write → the destination. Configure the collector’s targets, endpoint and authentication; changing application instrumentation alone is insufficient.

Metrics compatibility does not migrate Datadog dashboards, monitor semantics, logs or traces automatically. Inventory each signal and verify the required collector/exporter path before cutover.

Retention also needs review: the listed Datadog Pro metrics window is 15 months, while Grafana Pro lists 13 months for metrics and 30 days for logs and traces. Compare query results and alerts, not only whether samples arrive.

cost_math.result: $1,380 before logs, traces or RUM; Grafana Cloud Pro has no per-host infrastructure line

decision_matrix.situation: Series count scales with users, not hosts
decision_matrix.why: At 200,000 series the series meter bills $9,900 on Datadog against $1,175 on Grafana, and the 10,000-series allowance is account-wide.

decision_matrix.situation: A team already living in Datadog APM and security
decision_matrix.why: At 30 hosts the infrastructure plus APM licence is $1,380, and rebuilding dashboards and monitors is the hidden cost of leaving.

decision_matrix.situation: Five hosts and one person on call
decision_matrix.why: Datadog's licence starts at $75 for five hosts before any custom metrics; Grafana's platform fee is $19 for the account.

decision_matrix.situation: You need 15 months of full-resolution metrics
decision_matrix.why: Datadog keeps 15 months on Pro; Grafana Cloud Pro lists 13 months for metrics and 30 days for logs and traces.

decision_matrix.situation: The custom metrics line is already over $500
decision_matrix.why: That line is $500 per 10,000 series on Datadog and $65 per 10,000 on Grafana, so the same data crosses a factor of 7.7.

decision_matrix.situation: Logs are verbose JSON from a dozen services
decision_matrix.why: Datadog's index rate is per event and Grafana's is per GB, so 500 GB at 2.5 KB per event bills $550 against $247.50, and the same 500 GB at 250 bytes per event is 2 billion events, or $5,000 on the index line.

decision_matrix.situation: Security, SIEM and audit on one invoice
decision_matrix.why: Cloud SIEM, workload protection and audit trail are on the same price list; Grafana Cloud prices observability and leaves security elsewhere.

decision_matrix.situation: Everything is already Prometheus and you self-host Grafana
decision_matrix.why: Existing instrumentation may be reusable, but configure Prometheus or Alloy scraping and remote_write, then verify labels, queries, alerts and destination limits before switching.

verdict_summary: The modeled metrics bills favor Grafana Cloud, especially at high cardinality. That is not a complete migration cost: collector configuration, dashboards, alerts and non-metric signals need validation. Datadog may fit a team that relies on its integrated workflows; compare actual usage and transition work rather than assuming a fixed payback period.
migration_guide:
Keep compatible instrumentation, then build and test the collection pipeline. The Python client example below exposes a scrape target on port 9100; it is a cardinality anti-pattern demonstration, not a complete remote_write setup. Prometheus scrapes that target and forwards via remote_write, or Alloy connects prometheus.scrape to prometheus.remote_write.

Use the destination’s documented endpoint, tenant/account identifier and scoped authentication. Verify metric names, label mapping, histogram compatibility, scrape interval, sample timestamps, cardinality and ingestion limits. Watch failed sends, queue/WAL health, gaps and duplicate series during a limited parallel run.

Do not assume the Datadog Agent is a generic Prometheus remote_write forwarder. Confirm supported collection/export for each actual integration; logs and traces require their own paths. Review dashboards, alert queries and thresholds against observed results, establish rollback criteria, and retire the old path only after validation. No fixed quarter-long overlap or payback period is established here.

faqs.q: Are Grafana Cloud's tier prices marginal or flat?
faqs.a: Marginal. Each new band bills at a lower rate for the usage inside it, so the blended rate falls as the account grows: $6.50 per 1,000 to 100,000, then $5.90, then $5.50.

faqs.q: What exactly is a custom metric on Datadog?
faqs.a: A unique metric name plus tag combination, averaged hourly across the month. Adding a tag with many values multiplies the count even if the metric name never changes.

faqs.q: Does Grafana Cloud charge per host?
faqs.a: The Pro plan is a $19 platform fee per account. Host hours appear for Kubernetes monitoring at $0.01 per host hour, which is a separate product from infrastructure metrics.

faqs.q: Does a Prometheus client push directly to Grafana Cloud remote_write?
faqs.a: Not in the standard scrape-based setup. The client exposes /metrics; Prometheus scrapes it and forwards with remote_write, or Alloy uses prometheus.scrape feeding prometheus.remote_write. Configure the collector’s destination and authentication, then validate labels, gaps, duplicates, queries and alerts. The application example alone is not a complete pipeline.

hook: One hundred million requests that each take 200 ms and use 10 ms of CPU cost $147.80 on AWS Lambda and $51.40 on Cloudflare Workers. Nothing about the code differs. One vendor bills the waiting.

sections.title: Two vendors, three meters, two definitions of work
sections.content:
Lambda now publishes two price sheets. Event Functions bill requests plus duration in GB-seconds: $0.0000133334 per GB-second on Arm, $0.0000166667 on x86, and $0.20 per million requests. Web Functions bill active CPU at $0.0000276944 per vCPU-second, memory at $0.0000036667 per GB-second for as long as the environment exists, and $0.30 per million requests.

Workers bill one thing that matters: CPU milliseconds, $0.02 per million after 30 million included, plus $0.30 per million requests after 10 million on a $5 plan. The page is explicit that there is no charge for duration, for egress or for bandwidth.

| Meter | Lambda Event | Lambda Web | Workers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests | $0.20/M | $0.30/M | $0.30/M |
| Duration | GB-seconds | memory GB-s, whole life | none |
| CPU | inside duration | $0.0000276944/vCPU-s | $0.02/M CPU-ms |

sections.title: A GB-second is a memory meter wearing a clock
sections.content:
Duration billing multiplies wall time by allocated memory, and both factors are yours to set. A 512 MB function that takes 200 ms bills 0.5 GB × 0.2 s = 0.1 GB-s per request. At 100 million requests that is 10 million GB-seconds, or $133.34 on Arm at $0.0000133334.

Workers bills the 10 ms of actual work instead: 100 million × 10 ms = 1,000 million CPU-milliseconds, which is 970 million after the 30 million included, at $0.02 per million CPU-ms = $19.40.

So the ratio between the two vendors is not a rate difference. It is the fraction of the request that is CPU: 10 ms of 200 ms is 5%, and that 5% is what Workers meters. Make the handler heavier and the gap narrows; make it wait on a database and the gap widens.

sections.title: The bills cross at about 7.5 million requests
sections.content:
Same shape everywhere below: 200 ms duration, 512 MB, 10 ms of CPU, one function.

| Requests/month | Lambda Event (Arm) | Workers | Cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5M | $0.80 + $1.33 = $2.13 | $5.00 + $0.40 = $5.40 | Lambda |
| 7.5M | $1.30 + $4.67 = $5.97 | $5.00 + $0.90 = $5.90 | Workers, by 7¢ |
| 10M | $1.80 + $8.00 = $9.80 | $5.00 + $1.40 = $6.40 | Workers |
| 50M | $9.80 + $61.33 = $71.13 | $5.00 + $12.00 + $9.40 = $26.40 | Workers |
| 100M | $19.80 + $128.00 = $147.80 | $5.00 + $27.00 + $19.40 = $51.40 | Workers |

The crossover is a free-tier artefact, not a policy: 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds are free on Lambda, and 30 million CPU-ms are free on Workers. Below roughly 7.5 million requests the Lambda allowance is worth more than the CPU savings. Above it, the $5 plan floor disappears into the noise.

sections.title: Lambda's second sheet splits the same request in two
sections.content:
Web Functions are AWS's answer to active-CPU billing, and they price the same 100 million requests differently.

| Line | Lambda Event | Lambda Web | Workers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests | $19.80 | $30.00 | $27.00 |
| Compute | 10M GB-s = $128.00 | 1M vCPU-s = $27.69, 1.296M GB-s = $4.75 | 970M CPU-ms = $19.40 |
| Plan floor | — | — | $5.00 |
| **Total** | **$147.80** | **$62.45** | **$51.40** |

Web Functions bill $62.45 for the same traffic, 42% of the Event price, and still 21% above the Workers bill. The memory meter is why: it bills the environment for its whole life, idle time included, and AWS's own examples quietly assume exactly one environment stays up for the entire month.

sections.title: Where Lambda wins on the same sheet
sections.content:
The free allowance matters: in the stated 512 MB, 200 ms, 10 ms CPU model, 5 million requests cost $2.13 on Lambda and $5.40 on Workers. This assumes the allowances are not already consumed by other workloads.

Lambda supports up to 10,240 MB. Workers CPU limits vary by trigger; do not treat the HTTP limit as universal:

| Workers Paid invocation | CPU limit | Wall-clock limit |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | 30 s default; configurable to 5 min | No hard limit while client connected |
| Cron, interval under 1 hour | 30 s | 15 min |
| Cron, interval at least 1 hour | 15 min | 15 min |
| Queue consumer | 30 s default; configurable to 5 min | 15 min |

Queue wall time is not CPU time. Free and legacy plans have different limits; verify the deployed configuration. AWS integrations such as VPC, IAM, SQS and Kinesis may also outweigh a small compute-price difference.

sections.title: The exit door has a rewrite behind it
sections.content:
Correction, November 14, 2026: the wait-only example accidentally substituted 200 ms CPU for its stated 10 ms. At 10 million requests, Workers remains $6.40, not $44.40; the extra wall time changes Lambda’s duration bill only. Workers pricing and trigger limits were rechecked; other AWS figures retain their November 10 source check.

Moving runtimes still requires testing APIs, native dependencies, filesystem behavior and state bindings. Check the actual HTTP, Cron or Queue limit rather than assuming every invocation has a five-minute CPU cap.

The estimate covers one workload with available included usage, not a complete application invoice. Storage, queues, databases, retries and migration work can add costs; measure CPU and elapsed duration separately before choosing.

cost_math.result: $147.80 on Lambda against $51.40 on Workers

cost_math.result: $62.45, 58% below Lambda's own Event price for identical traffic

cost_math.label: Cross-over against Lambda's free tier
cost_math.result: Equal at about 7.5M requests a month; below that Lambda's free allowance wins, above it the CPU meter does

cost_math.result: Lambda rises from $9.80 to $63.13 (+$53.33); Workers stays $6.40. All stated allowances are assumed available; taxes and other services are excluded.

decision_matrix.situation: Under about 5 million requests a month
decision_matrix.why: The 1M-request and 400,000 GB-second free allowances cover the whole job: 5M requests at 200 ms and 512 MB price at $2.13 against $5.40 on Workers.

decision_matrix.situation: 100 million requests that mostly wait on I/O
decision_matrix.why: The same shape prices at $51.40 against $147.80, because 10 ms of CPU out of a 200 ms request is all Workers meters.

decision_matrix.situation: A function that needs 10 GB of memory
decision_matrix.why: Lambda supports up to 10,240 MB; Workers uses a much smaller isolate memory budget. CPU limits are separate and depend on the invocation type.

decision_matrix.situation: Long-lived streaming to a browser
decision_matrix.why: Active-CPU billing ignores the wait: AWS's own LLM streaming example prices 5M requests of 3 s at $33.94, against $101.00 as Event Functions.

decision_matrix.situation: Byte-heavy responses at the edge
decision_matrix.why: Workers charges nothing for egress or bandwidth, and static asset requests are free and unlimited.

decision_matrix.situation: SQS, Kinesis, VPC and IAM already wired into the app
decision_matrix.why: The compute line is often the small one; rewriting event sources and IAM to leave AWS costs more than the difference on the invoice.

decision_matrix.situation: A cron job every hour, minutes of CPU each
decision_matrix.why: At an hourly interval, paid Cron permits up to 15 minutes CPU and 15 minutes wall time. The 720-invocation × 180,000 ms example is $5 + (129.6M − 30M) × $0.02/M = $6.992, about $6.99, assuming no other usage or services.

decision_matrix.situation: Traffic so spiky that one environment cannot serve it
decision_matrix.why: Web Functions bill memory for the life of every environment, and the pricing examples quietly assume exactly one environment runs all month.

verdict_summary: For a request that waits, Workers is two to three times cheaper and the gap grows with every millisecond you spend on a database call. For a request that works, the two converge, and Lambda's free tier and memory ceiling win back the low end. The bill is a statement about your code's shape, not about the vendors' rates.
migration_guide:
Lambda to Workers is a runtime rewrite: the handler becomes a fetch listener, environment variables become bindings, and anything that needs a native module, a spawned process or a writable disk has no equivalent. State moves to Durable Objects or KV, which bill separately.

Workers to Lambda is smaller but not free: package the code, replace KV and Durable Objects with a database, and accept that egress is metered again. In both directions the traffic analysis comes first, because the arithmetic only favours one vendor when you know the request duration and the CPU share of it.

faqs.q: Does no duration charge mean Workers has no execution limit?
faqs.a: No. Standard Workers bills CPU and requests rather than elapsed duration, but trigger limits still apply. Paid HTTP CPU defaults to 30 seconds and can be configured to 5 minutes. Paid Cron CPU is 30 seconds below a one-hour interval and 15 minutes at intervals of at least one hour. Queue CPU defaults to 30 seconds, configurable to 5 minutes; its separate wall-clock limit is 15 minutes.

faqs.q: What are Lambda Web Functions?
faqs.a: A second Lambda billing model that charges per request, per vCPU-second of active CPU and per GB-second of memory for as long as the execution environment exists.

faqs.q: What happens if a request waits longer but still uses 10 ms CPU?
faqs.a: In the stated 10M-request paid-plan model with available allowances, increasing wall time from 200 ms to 1 s leaves Workers at $6.40. Lambda Event Arm at 512 MB rises from $9.80 to $63.13. The old $44.40 Workers result incorrectly used 200 ms CPU. These are modeled costs, not measured performance or complete invoices.

faqs.q: Is a cold start billed?
faqs.a: On Event Functions the initialisation runs inside the billed duration, and SnapStart adds its own cache and restore charges. Workers does not bill duration at all.

hook: Resend and SendGrid offer similar entry prices, but trial expiry and overage billing change the bill. Resend’s paid overages need opt-in and round up in 1,000-email buckets. A standard SendGrid trial ends with sending paused, not an automatic paid subscription.

sections.title: At 100,000 emails, the feature tiers cost more
sections.content:
The listed 100,000-email tiers have a $55 feature-tier step, not an increase in included volume. This does not make the feature bundles equivalent or establish why either vendor set its prices.

| At 100,000 emails | Entry tier | Feature tier | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resend | Pro $35 | Scale $90 | $55 |
| SendGrid | Essentials $34.95 | Pro $89.95 | $55 |

All figures here are USD monthly estimates before taxes and add-ons. Check your actual account quote, especially for reseller or custom-contract plans.

sections.title: The ladder is not monotonic, and overage is sometimes the cheaper rung
sections.content:
Resend paid transactional plans can opt into Transactional Overages in Settings; Free cannot. Without opt-in, quota limits apply rather than this paid continuation.

Formula: base + ceil(max(0, usage − quota) / 1,000) × plan bucket rate. At $20 for 50,000 and $0.90 per extra bucket:

| Monthly usage | Rounded extra buckets | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 50,003 | 1 | $20.90 |
| 51,415 | 2 | $21.80 |
| 66,000 | 16 | $34.40 |
| 66,001 | 17 | $35.30 |

The $35/100,000 tier first becomes cheaper at 66,001 emails, not 66,666. Count all usage charged to the quota, not just outbound messages; taxes and other fees are extra.

With opt-in, the listed $35/100,000 plan plus 100 extra buckets totals $125 for 200,000 emails, below the $160 Scale tier but without its features. Do not apply Resend’s rounding or activation rule to SendGrid.

sections.title: Dedicated IP: $30 plus a $55 step, or included at $89.95
sections.content:
A dedicated IP may matter for a sustained high-volume sender, but it does not by itself guarantee better delivery. Choose it based on sending patterns and operational needs.

Resend sells it as a $30 per month add-on, and only on Scale, to accounts sending more than 3,000 emails a day. At 100,000 emails that is $90 + $30 = $120, or $1.20 per 1,000.

SendGrid includes one dedicated IP in Pro, which is $89.95 at the same volume, or $0.90 per 1,000.

| 100,000 emails with a dedicated IP | Monthly | Per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|
| Resend Scale + IP add-on | $120.00 | $1.20 |
| SendGrid Pro | $89.95 | $0.90 |

There is no Resend Pro path to an IP in the listed self-service tiers. That is not a worse deal; it is a missing SKU, and it decides the vendor for anyone whose deliverability depends on one.

sections.title: Domain authentication is table stakes; the domain count is not
sections.content:
Both authenticate sending with DKIM, SPF and DMARC, and both include a REST API, SMTP relay and official SDKs on every paid plan. The differences are in the quantities.

| Quantity | Resend | SendGrid |
|---|---|---|
| Custom domains | 3 Free, 10 Pro, 1,000 Scale | Domain authentication included |
| Extra domains | $20/mo adds 100 | Not a listed line item |
| Teammates | Not metered | 1 on Essentials, 1,000 on Pro |
| Event webhooks | 5 on Pro, 10 on Scale | 2 on Essentials, 5 on Pro |
| SSO | $150/mo add-on on Scale | Included in Pro |

An agency managing dozens of client domains should price the domain line before the email line: Resend's add-on covers 100 extra domains for $20, and SendGrid's inclusion has no printed ceiling.

sections.title: A trial ending is not an automatic subscription
sections.content:
Correction, November 14, 2026: the earlier article wrongly described automatic SendGrid paid conversion and continuous per-email Resend overage billing. The calculations and FAQ are corrected.

A standard new direct SendGrid/Twilio Email API account gets a 60-day trial at 100 emails/day. After expiry, sending stops unless you choose a paid upgrade; the trial does not itself trigger a $19.95 charge. Email API and Marketing Campaigns are separate plans.

Partner/reseller accounts such as Azure can differ: check actual terms and notices. Older direct free accounts are not a guaranteed exemption; Twilio announced their retirement in May 2025 with a transition to paused sending absent upgrade. Already-paid subscriptions follow their own terms.

Resend’s free tier allows 3,000 emails/month and 100/day. $19.95 × 12 = $239.40 represents twelve voluntarily purchased SendGrid months, not a trial-expiry bill or a first year including the trial.

sections.title: Where each one breaks
sections.content:
Resend breaks on the feature boundary. The dedicated IP, SSO and 1,000 domains all sit on Scale, so the 100,000-email customer who outgrows Pro pays a $55 step and then $30 more for the IP. Marketing email moves to a separate contact-priced plan, and broadcasts only reach existing contacts.

SendGrid breaks on the tier edge and on history. The 50,000 Essentials tier charges $1.33 per 1,000 beyond its volume, so 80,000 emails bills $19.95 + $39.90 = $59.85 against $34.95 for the next tier up. Searchable activity is 3 days on Essentials against 7 on Pro, so a deliverability investigation can outlast the evidence.

Check three numbers before choosing: your monthly volume rounded up to the rung that covers it, whether you need an IP this quarter, and how many domains you will authenticate in a year.

cost_math.label: 100,000 emails a month, no dedicated IP
cost_math.result: $35.00 against $34.95, a five-cent gap at the bottom of the ladder

sections.title: Two billing models, both with usage meters
sections.content:
Correction, November 14, 2026: this article previously treated Supabase Postgres Changes as unmetered and compared a high-fan-out workload with a flat $25 project. Supabase bills Realtime Messages separately from database compute, so that conclusion is withdrawn.

A database query and delivery of a Realtime change are different billing events. Supabase combines plan, compute and usage charges; Firestore Standard meters document operations, among other items.

| Meter | Published unit | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Firestore Standard reads | $0.03/100,000 | us-central1, not every edition or region |
| Firestore Standard writes | $0.09/100,000 | Same regional model |
| Supabase Realtime | 5M messages included on Pro, then $2.50/M | Organization allowance; excess rounded up in 1M packages |
| Supabase Pro Micro base | $25 + $10 − $10 credit | One project, excludes usage overage |

sections.title: Model deliveries before comparing prices
sections.content:
Assume 50 clients continuously watch the same 100 documents; every document changes 20 times/minute for 30 days. Each change reaches all 50 clients, with no coalescing, filtering or missed deliveries.

50 × 100 × 20 × 60 × 24 × 30 = 4.32 billion deliveries. Firestore Standard read-only gross cost at the stated rate is $1,296. This is arithmetic, not a load-test result.

Firestore bills listener additions and updates, plus removals caused by document changes; deleting a document does not itself add a listener read. Reconnects can reissue billed queries: always with offline persistence disabled, or after more than 30 minutes disconnected with it enabled.

Initial reads, reconnects, security-rule and index reads, storage, transfer and taxes are omitted. The underlying 86.4M updates would also incur writes: $77.76 gross at $0.09/100,000. Daily free quotas must be applied by day; unused quota is not a monthly pool.

sections.title: Supabase messages, spend caps and throughput are separate
sections.content:
Postgres Changes counts one message per receiving client: one change delivered to 50 clients means 50 messages. Broadcast also counts the send plus each receiving client; Presence has its own traffic, so do not substitute one meter for another.

At 4.32B delivered messages, ceil((4.32B − 5M)/1M) × $2.50 = $10,787.50 overage. Adding the illustrative $25 Pro Micro base gives $10,812.50, before extra compute, egress, connections or other usage.

The model averages 1,666.7 deliveries/s. Published Pro limits are 500 messages/s, or 2,500/s for Pro without a spend cap; peak connections are 500 or 10,000 respectively. These are Realtime limits, not database pooler connections.

A spend cap covers Realtime quota overage: leaving it on can restrict service, not grant unlimited free delivery. Turning it off permits charges but does not remove throughput limits or prove capacity; validate burst load, payloads, RLS work and actual project settings.

sections.title: Index entry reads are the Firestore line item nobody quotes
sections.content:
- One read per batch of up to 1,000 index entries a query reads.
- A query with **one** range field pays nothing for index entries. Zero range fields are also exempt. Add a second range field and billing starts.
- `count()`, `sum()` and `avg()` bill index reads, with a 1-document-read minimum even at zero entries.

Firestore's own docs give the example: `count()` over 1,500 index entries bills 2 document reads.

> Ten million plain reads cost $3.00 at the listed rate. The `count()` in your page header is a different bill.

Audit any query that combines two range fields before it ships.

sections.title: Migration is a schema project with a script attached
sections.content:
`supabase-community/firebase-to-supabase` on GitHub is community tooling, not an official CLI. It exports collections and loads tables; splitting nested JSON into related tables needs custom hooks.

Auth is the sharper edge. `firestoreusers2json` and `import_users` move users, importing hashes with Firestore's SCRYPT parameters (`base64_signer_key`, `base64_salt_separator`, `rounds`, `mem_cost`).

> Verifying an existing Firebase password on first login needs a middleware the repo itself marks **work in progress**. The AWS Lambda variant is listed as TBD.

Until that middleware exists, plan for blocked logins at cutover and decide in advance whether you force a password reset.

sections.title: Compare complete bills and prove capacity
sections.content:
Do not choose either platform from the old $1,296-versus-$25 headline. The corrected model makes Supabase message overage much larger than the Firestore read line, but neither is a full bill or performance guarantee.

1. Measure changes, actual recipients, payload sizes, active hours and reconnects.
2. Include Supabase Realtime packages and other usage, not only Postgres compute.
3. Include Firestore writes, query/security-rule reads, storage and network costs for the selected region and edition.
4. Load-test throughput, burst behavior and authorization overhead before sizing a project.
5. Consider batching, narrower subscriptions or lower update frequency when product requirements allow.

Firestore free allowances include 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes daily, plus storage/network quotas. Supabase’s included Realtime quota is also finite; check consumption across the organization.

faqs.q: Does offset pagination save reads on Firestore?
faqs.a: No. Firestore bills a read for every skipped document, so offset 10 returning 1 document costs 11 reads.

faqs.q: Does disabling the Supabase spend cap guarantee this load works?

faqs.q: How is Firestore vector search billed?
faqs.a: kNN vector search bills one read per batch of up to 100 vector index entries. That is a tenth of the 1,000-entry batch size used for regular index entry reads.

sections.title: Vercel runs your framework; Cloudflare runs your requests
sections.content:
Vercel runs your framework and bills for what it delivers. Cloudflare runs your requests and bills for what they execute.

- Vercel: past Pro's 1 TB Fast Data Transfer and 10M CDN requests, every GB costs from $0.15 and every million requests from $2.
- Cloudflare: egress costs $0, but Workers Paid charges $0.30 per million requests past 10M and $0.02 per million CPU-ms past 30M.

Prices are the vendors' listed rates as of 10 November 2026; Vercel's overages are starting rates, and examples credited to Cloudflare are Cloudflare's own.

> At 3 TB a month the gap is $307.20 of Vercel transfer overage; at 50M requests it is $80 versus $12 of request overage.

Before moving, check each handler against Workers' listed limits: 10 ms CPU per invocation on Free, and a 30-second default with a 5-minute maximum of CPU time on Paid.

sections.title: An idle await no longer chooses the winner
sections.content:
Fluid compute, the default for new Vercel projects, bills active CPU rather than wall time, and Workers bills CPU-ms. An idle `await` burns no CPU meter on either; it does not make the whole deployment free.

- Vercel Fluid compute: Active CPU starts at $0.128/vCPU-hour.
- Vercel says provisioned memory is billed in GB-hours at less than 10% of the Active CPU rate.

In-function concurrency lets concurrent requests share one instance; Vercel claims up to 85% savings from it and up to 90% from Active CPU pricing.

> Workers Paid includes 30M CPU-ms a month; Vercel bills Active CPU and provisioned memory as separate metered lines.

Waiting on an external API no longer establishes a CPU-price reason to migrate; inspect transfer and request counts before touching the runtime.

sections.title: The penalty moved to bytes and requests
sections.content:
Vercel penalizes byte-heavy delivery and request fan-out after allowances; Cloudflare penalizes uncached CPU work and paid requests, not egress.

| Monthly workload | Vercel Pro | Cloudflare Workers Paid |
|---|---|---|
| 3 TB transfer | 2,048 GB over × $0.15/GB = $307.20 | $0 egress |
| 50M requests, overage | 40M CDN requests × $2/M = $80 | 40M × $0.30/M = $12 |
| Same, with plan floor | $20 × 1 seat + $80 = $100 | $5 + $12 = $17 |
| 1M CPU-ms | $0.128 ÷ 3.6M × 1M ≈ $0.0356, before memory | $0.02 after 30M included |

The request rows apply only to requests that run a Worker; Vercel's line counts CDN requests, while Cloudflare static asset requests are free and unlimited.

> Teams serving 3 TB a month or 50M Worker requests should not pick Vercel Pro: they pay $307.20 against $0, or $100 against $17 before CPU.

sections.title: The asset limit can stop the deployment first
sections.content:
Consider a static export containing a downloadable asset larger than 25 MiB. Cloudflare Pages rejects that deployment shape on its asset ceiling; cheap transfer cannot rescue it.

- Pages builds per month: 500 Free / 5,000 Pro / 20,000 Business, with 1 / 5 / 20 concurrent; 20,000 files per site on Free; 100 projects per account.
- Pages: 20-minute build timeout; 25 MiB maximum per asset.

Exceeding an included traffic allowance raises a bill; exceeding an asset ceiling breaks the deployment plan. Teams whose build runs past 20 minutes should not pick Pages until the build is split, and teams deploying more than 500 times a month need Pages Pro's 5,000.

> Shrink or remove every asset over 25 MiB before targeting Pages; a Vercel function that needs more than 5 minutes must be split, or checked against Workers' 5-minute CPU-time cap.

sections.title: Caching cuts Cloudflare's CPU line; requests still bill
sections.content:
Cloudflare charges $0 for egress, but Pages Functions still bill as Workers requests and CPU-ms. D1 and R2 carry their own line items.

Cloudflare's own example uses 100M requests at 7 ms CPU each; Workers Caching at 80% hits changes the CPU bill:

- Without caching: (100M × 7 − 30M) CPU-ms × $0.02/M CPU-ms = $13.40.
- With caching: (100M × (1 − 80%) × 7 − 30M) CPU-ms × $0.02/M CPU-ms = $2.20.

Cache hits still cost a request, but no CPU in Cloudflare's example.

> The request line stays at (100M − 10M) × $0.30/M = $27.00, so the cached total is $5.00 + $27.00 + $2.20 = $34.20 against $45.40 uncached.

Only count that saving for responses your app can safely reuse; a lower hit rate moves the bill back toward $45.40.

sections.title: Above 1 TB or 10M requests, Vercel Pro is the expensive host
sections.content:
- A team above 1 TB or 10M CDN requests a month should move to Cloudflare Pages: at 3 TB that removes $307.20 of overage.
- A team whose Vercel deployment works inside both Pro allowances should stay: the bill to beat is $20 per seat plus Active CPU and memory.
- A team with CPU-heavy handlers inside Workers' CPU cap should move: $0.02 per million CPU-ms beats Vercel's starting ≈ $0.0356.
- A team adding seats faster than traffic pays Vercel $20 per seat against Workers Paid's $5 per-account minimum; it should move after confirming Pages Pro and Business prices.

> Pages allows 500 builds a month on Free, and each build must finish within 20 minutes.

Count seats at $20 each, check your longest build against Pages' 20-minute timeout and check your largest asset against 25 MiB.

sections.title: Your editor budget now buys a different contract
sections.content:
A renewal priced on the old $20 tier now buys either $8 Plus, which is Grok-only, or $30 Premium, where Claude and GPT tokens bill at API list price on top.

Two questions decide it: do you need non-Grok models, and does your review happen in GitHub PRs?

> Cursor told Reuters it runs at about $2.6B annualised revenue; SpaceX bought it in an all-stock deal at a $60B valuation.

Cursor's ownership changed before this renewal decision. Cursor is now a wholly owned SpaceX subsidiary.

- 21 April 2026: SpaceX and Cursor announced a partnership with a $10B payment and a $60B acquisition option.
- 16 June 2026: SpaceX signed the all-stock deal at a $60B valuation.
- 14 August 2026: the deal closed; Cursor joined the SpaceXAI team (SpaceX absorbed xAI in February 2026) to work on Grok, Grok Build, Grok Bot, Grok API and Cursor.

> Cursor states its constraint was compute: “We've wanted to push our training efforts much further, but we've been bottlenecked by compute.”

sections.title: Model ownership and repository ownership impose different limits
sections.content:
**Cursor's philosophy: the model is the product**, so the editor owns the model and the inference bill. Its own price sheet says so — Plus at $8 offers only Grok models, while Premium opens third-party access billed separately at API list price.

**GitHub sells the repository**, so Copilot's AI lands in PRs and reviews. That forbids giving review away: Free gets agent mode and the CLI, but PR review waits for the $10 Pro tier.

Cursor pushes back on that line — Premium lists code hosting via Origin and AI code review via Bugbot — but the two still compete on different surfaces: Cursor's $8 Plus cannot run Claude or GPT, and Copilot Free cannot review a PR.

sections.title: The meters punish different habits
sections.content:
Cursor's meter punishes third-party model use specifically: no plan includes those tokens, so Claude or GPT work passes through at API list price. Copilot's meter is a single credit pool per user that agent mode, review, cloud and CLI all drain.

| Vendor's monthly offer | Usage that incurs the penalty |
|---|---|
| Cursor: $8 Plus; $30 Premium | Plus is Grok-only; Premium adds third-party models at API list price on top |
| GitHub Copilot: $10 Pro ($15 credits); $39 Pro+ ($70 credits, Opus included); $100 Max ($200 credits) | Agent mode, review, cloud, CLI and app consume the same credit meter |

When a Copilot seat exhausts its credits, Pro and above buy extra.

| Buyer | Cursor | GitHub Copilot |
|---|---|---|
| 10 seats | Teams 10 × $30 = $300/month | Pro 10 × $10 = $100/month |
| Claude-dependent developer | Premium $30 plus metered tokens | Pro+ $39 with $70 of credits |
| Heavy user | Super $100 (15× Plus) | Max $100 ($200 credits) |

sections.title: Model neutrality now needs a renewal check
sections.content:
Teams that chose Cursor partly to stay model-agnostic now buy from a company whose model is Grok. Ownership changed the incentive. It does not prove that every request routes to Grok.

> Cursor states that Grok 4.6, the first joint model, scores between 69.9% and 70.8% on CursorBench and 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

Before renewing, replay representative repository tasks and record the separately billed third-party usage.

- On Premium, compare the separate third-party token charge with the Claude or GPT work your team believes it ran; a near-zero charge means that work did not run on third-party models.
- Do not buy Plus if non-Grok access is a requirement; test Premium's unbundled bill before committing.

sections.title: Copilot Free runs the agent; PR review costs $10

GitHub's counter-argument is reach: Copilot runs in VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse, Neovim, Zed and on github.com. Copilot Free already supports agent mode and the CLI, with limited usage.

- Copilot in the cloud starts at Pro.
- PR review, file diff review and custom instructions start at Pro.
- Assigning work to Copilot so it creates a pull request also starts at Pro.

A successful CLI trial does not establish that Free can perform your review workflow.

> Pro's $15 of monthly credits per user ($10 base + $5 flex) funds agent mode, code review and cloud work alike.

Try the actual handoff from assigned work to reviewed PR before migrating the team.

sections.content:
Teams happy on Grok should buy Cursor; teams whose review lives in GitHub PRs should buy Copilot Pro. Cursor's $8 Plus undercuts Copilot Pro by $2, but only if Grok is enough.

- Choose Cursor if Grok meets your workload and third-party usage is optional.
- Choose GitHub Copilot if review and assigned PR work matter more than owning a separate editor workflow.

Moving to Copilot puts custom instructions (`.instructions.md`) and PR review behind Pro; moving to Cursor puts Claude and GPT behind list-price billing.

> If you need Claude inside a known monthly allotment, Copilot Pro+ at $39 includes Opus within $70 of credits; Cursor bills third-party tokens at API list price on top of $30 Premium.

Today, list the workflows that need Claude or GPT and price them on both plans.

sections.title: Notion sells a server with a meter; Obsidian sells a folder with a pipe
sections.content:
**Obsidian sells a folder.** Plain Markdown on your disk, no server, no meter, and the app itself is free without limits. **Notion sells shared state.** Permissions, databases and agents live on their servers, and everything around them carries a budget: page history, uploads, API calls, agent credits.

**Obsidian: notes are files on your disk**, and Obsidian states the app is free without limits, with no telemetry.

- **Notion makes history a plan feature.** Notion page history is 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus and 90 on Business.
- Obsidian has no permission model, no server-side agent and no built-in multi-user editing; collaboration requires Sync shared vaults or third-party tooling.

sections.title: Friday recovery: does the version you need still exist?
sections.content:
On Friday afternoon, test recovery before choosing a plan: does the version from before the mistaken edit still exist?

| Plan | Price | Page history |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0/member | 7 days |
| Plus | $10/member/month | 30 days |
| Business | $20/member/month | 90 days |

The pattern this punishes is the slow mistake. Choose a window that covers how long a mistake could go unnoticed.

The rest of Free's ceiling sits in the same place:

- File uploads capped at **5 MB** (Plus raises it to 5 GB).
- **10 external guests**.
- A Free-plan workspace block limit that Notion announced for 2026-09-08.

Obsidian has no window to buy. A vault is plain files, so `git log` keeps every committed version for as long as you keep the repo.

sections.title: Bases adds views, not permissions: who should not pick Obsidian
sections.content:
Bases is a **core plugin**, not a community add-on. It renders database views over frontmatter properties, and the data stays in your Markdown files.

- Table and Cards: 1.9
- List and Map: 1.10 (Map needs the Maps plugin)
- Kanban: 1.14

The `.base` file is YAML and holds only the view definition:

```yaml
filters:
  and:
    - file.inFolder("Projects")
    - file.hasTag("active")
formulas:
  ratio: '(price / age).toFixed(2)'
views:
  - type: table
    order:
      - file.name
      - formula.ratio
```

Obsidian's own docs: "Delete a base and your notes are untouched." What Bases still does not give you:

- **Permissions.** Obsidian has no permission model.
- **Server-side computed properties.** Bases does not replace them.
- **Multi-user edit.** Shared vaults sync files; there is no built-in co-editing.

Do not pick Obsidian if you need granular database permissions or built-in multi-user editing.

sections.title: Notion's agent is real, and so is its meter
sections.content:
Notion's built-in agent lives on Business at $20/member/month, next to AI Meeting Notes. Free and Plus get an AI trial only.

| Notion piece | Billing, per Notion |
|---|---|
| Notion Agent | Included in Business |
| Custom Agents | "Free to try, then $10 per 1,000 monthly Notion credits" |
| Workers | Beta: custom code for agent tools and sync |

Custom Agents are separately metered; do not infer a Business prerequisite. Obsidian has no server-side agent.

Notion API budgets:

- **180 requests per 60-second window per connection**, or **600/minute on Business/Enterprise**; bursts allowed.
- A **per-workspace** budget shared by every connection; its `Retry-After` can exceed a minute. It scales by plan.
- Data-source queries capped near 3 requests/second per connection.

Obey `Retry-After` on HTTP 429 or 529 (`service_overload`); the JS SDK retries for you.

sections.title: For ten people, $2,400 a year buys permissions or it buys nothing
sections.content:
Run the 10-person team through both price sheets:

- For 10 people needing Business permissions and Notion Agent, 10 × $20 × 12 = **$2,400/year**.
- For 10 people needing Plus's 30-day history, 10 × $10 × 12 = **$1,200/year**.
- For 10 people wanting Obsidian Sync, 10 × $4 × 12 = **$480/year**, billed annually.
- For 10 people choosing Sync plus optional commercial licences, (10 × $4 × 12) + (10 × $50) = **$980/year**.

Business includes:

- SAML SSO, granular database permissions, private teamspaces.
- 90-day page history and the Notion Agent.

Do not pay for Business solely to store private drafts if you do not need its agent, AI Meeting Notes, SSO, permissions or 90-day page history.

> For 10 people, the app bill is $0 with git or iCloud instead of Sync and no optional licences; choosing licences adds 10 × $50 = $500/year.

sections.title: Choose by permissions, then test recovery
sections.content:
Choose Notion Business when granular database permissions or private teamspaces are required; choose Obsidian for local Markdown notes only if you can forgo a permission model and built-in multi-user editing.

Check these today:

1. Open page history on your most important Notion page. Can you recover the version from before a mistaken edit within your plan's 7-, 30- or 90-day window?
2. Identify the Business permissions, private teamspaces, agent or recovery window you need.
3. List every integration calling the Notion API. Check connection, workspace and data-source query budgets before upgrading.
4. On Obsidian at work, explicitly accept or decline the optional commercial licence.

Choose Obsidian for local Markdown notes if you can forgo permissions and built-in multi-user editing: the app costs $0, while Sync for 10 people costs 10 × $4 × 12 = $480/year billed annually. Obsidian to Notion is worse in the other direction: plain files become blocks, the API becomes a 180-request-per-minute budget, and your git history stops being your history. Decide by which of those two losses you can actually live with.

sections.content:
Bun is MIT. Node.js is MIT. Neither sells a paid tier, so the bill is engineer-hours on three meters: the release calendar, the compatibility surface and the native-module ABI.

> For teams maintaining a Node service: as of 10 November 2026, both runtimes have no price.

- **Node:** Node publishes a release calendar; v26 Lithium, v24 Krypton and v22 Jod are LTS.
- **Bun:** 1.4.0 (20 August 2026) combined the Rust rewrite with the compatibility-target move from 24.3.0 to 26.3.0 and native ABI 147.

For Bun 1.4, check whether your native addons have builds for `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` 147.

sections.title: Node bills you on a date you did not choose
sections.content:
Node's release page reads like a work schedule:

| Major | Status | Key date |
|---|---|---|
| v27 | Alpha | first released 29 Oct 2026 |
| v26 Lithium | LTS | first released 5 May 2026 |
| v25 | EOL | 31 Mar 2026 |
| v24 Krypton | LTS | first released 6 May 2025 |
| v22 Jod | LTS | first released 24 Apr 2024 |
| v20 Iron | EOL | 24 Mar 2026 |

Support window and release cycle:

1. LTS "typically guarantees that critical bugs will be fixed for a total of 30 months" (Node's wording).
2. Starting with v27, the cycle becomes annual: every major gets six months of Alpha, six of Current, then LTS.

Read it as a penalty table. It punishes the team that adopts a major and forgets it: v20 lived from 17 Apr 2023 to 24 Mar 2026, about 35 months.

> If production still runs Node 20, plan a move to Node 24 or 26 LTS: Node 20 reached EOL on 24 March 2026.

sections.title: Who should not pick Node for unbuilt TypeScript
sections.content:
Type stripping is on by default, stable since v25.2.0 / v24.12.0. Node executes erasable syntax without type checking; other syntax needs separate tooling.

```ts
// runs on Node 26 with no flags: every annotation here is erasable
type Host = string;
const host: Host = process.env.HOST ?? "localhost";
console.log(`binding ${host}`);
```

> `enum` throws `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`.

Node 26 also refuses:

- `namespace` with runtime code, parameter properties, import aliases: same error
- `.tsx` files
- `paths`, because `tsconfig.json` is ignored
- TypeScript inside `node_modules`
- parsing without WebAssembly: `ERR_WEBASSEMBLY_NOT_SUPPORTED`

This meter punishes codebases built on enums and path aliases; for them, the build step stays.

sections.title: Bun's own node:http count leaves 415 − 403 = 12 tests failing
sections.content:
Bun says it plainly: "Bun is not 100% compatible with Node.js yet." Bun's own 1.4 counts against the Node 26.3.0 suite:

| Module | Bun 1.4 passes | Not passing |
|---|---|---|
| node:http | 403 / 415 | 415 − 403 = 12 |
| node:fs | 349 / 358 | 358 − 349 = 9 |
| node:module | 68 / 93 | 93 − 68 = 25 |
| node:test_runner | 28 / 81 | 81 − 28 = 53 |
| node:inspector | 22 / 110 | 110 − 22 = 88 |
| node:sqlite | 18 / 18 | 18 − 18 = 0 |

On node:http that is 12 ÷ 415 ≈ 2.9%, the failing 3%. Bun says 1.4 made 1,517 more Node tests pass.

> The ABI tax: 1.4 moved the compatibility target from 24.3.0 to 26.3.0. `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` is now 147, so native addons built for Node 24 must be rebuilt.

Check required inspector APIs; module pass counts are not application coverage.

sections.title: Who should not pick Bun: teams requiring missing APIs
sections.content:
Bun's compatibility docs name the gaps. Map each to a service you run:

- **HTTP servers tuned for a load balancer.** `http.Server` does not extend `net.Server`, the `keepAlive` / `keepAliveInitialDelay` server options are no-ops, and `listen(handle)` is ignored. Your keep-alive tuning silently does nothing.
- **mTLS and multi-tenant TLS.** node:https lacks `getPeerCertificate()` and `getCipher()` and does not support `SNICallback`. Retain Node if you require these APIs.
- **Signing code.** BoringSSL-backed node:crypto lacks `ed448`, `x448`, `rsa-pss` and `dsa` keys, has no `secp256k1` curve and no `chacha20-poly1305`.
- **APM tracing.** `async_hooks` `createHook` is a stub and async ids are always 0; correlation by async id collapses.
- **`cluster` fleets on macOS or Windows.** HTTP load-balancing across workers only works on Linux, via `SO_REUSEPORT`.

> `AsyncLocalStorage` context does not propagate into Worker/BroadcastChannel events in Bun.

sections.title: Bun stays MIT after Anthropic's acquisition; check before migrating
sections.content:
Anthropic acquired Bun on 2 December 2025. Claude Code ships as a Bun executable (Bun's statement), and Bun's founder wrote then: "Today, Bun makes $0 in revenue." Bun stays MIT.

The acquisition changes who pays for Bun's roadmap. It does not change the licence, and it does not change the API surface you have to test.

Check today:

1. List every `.node` addon in the tree and whether it has a build for `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` 147.
2. Check required HTTP APIs, `createHook`, distinct async IDs, `getPeerCertificate` and `SNICallback` against Bun's gaps.
3. Write down the EOL date of the Node major running in production.

migration_guide: Moving to Bun starts with `bun install` reading the same package.json, but every native addon needs a build for NODE_MODULE_VERSION 147 before it loads, so the hook stampede is the first thing to schedule. Moving back is not automatic either: Bun's compatibility docs list the API gaps you will meet — getPeerCertificate(), SNICallback, async_hooks — and there is no tool that rewrites handlers around them. Run the service test suite under both runtimes before either direction, then keep the loser's addon builds around for a release or two.

faqs.q: Does Node 26 type-check TypeScript?
faqs.a: No: type stripping performs no type checking, so a separate tool is still required. Decorators are a parser error, and `--experimental-transform-types` was removed in v26.0.0.

faqs.q: Is Bun faster than Node?
faqs.a: Bun's own `hello.js` benchmark puts Linux start-up at 5.1 ms for Bun 1.4 versus 27.2 ms for Node.js 26; these are vendor measurements, not independent ones. Separately, Bun's peak-memory figures under load, with 1,000,000 requests and 64 connections, put the Vite dev server at 233 MB on Bun versus 214 MB on Node, so Bun is not lighter everywhere.

faqs.q: Can I buy support for a Node major after LTS ends?
faqs.a: Not from the Node.js project itself. Commercial support past Maintenance LTS is sold by OpenJS Ecosystem Sustainability Program partners.

faqs.q: Does Bun's MIT licence cover everything in the binary?
faqs.a: No: Bun statically links JavaScriptCore/WebKit, which is LGPL-2. That is why Bun's licence file spells out relinking obligations.

sections.title: Free ORMs, separate hosting bills and dependency risk
sections.content:
If you are choosing between Prisma's generated client and Drizzle's TypeScript schema, separate the free ORM decision from database pricing and release-candidate risk.

- **Prisma:** generates its Rust-free client with `prisma-client`; queries pass through a TypeScript/WebAssembly compiler and a JS driver adapter.
- **Drizzle:** the TypeScript file is the schema, without client codegen or a schema DSL; `drizzle-kit` generates migrations.

> Prisma's model forbids skipping the build: no generator run, no client. Drizzle's forbids a schema outside TypeScript, and Drizzle states its relational API "always outputs exactly 1 SQL query".

sections.title: Who should not pick Prisma: teams avoiding client generation
sections.content:
Prisma 7.0.0 shipped 19 November 2025 with a Rust-free client: a TypeScript/WebAssembly query compiler plus a JS driver adapter.

- Prisma 7.10.1 shipped 15 October 2026: generator `output` is required, replacing generation into `node_modules` by default.
- The upgrade guide replaces the old datasource URL style with `prisma.config.ts`.

Prisma's AMA of 13 February 2026 attributes "cases where throughput is similar or slightly worse" to database access from JavaScript instead of a multi-threaded Rust runtime.

> Since 7.3.0, `$queryRaw` and `$executeRaw` skip the compiler entirely.

Avoid Prisma if client generation is a blocker.

sections.title: Who should not pick Drizzle: teams ruling out its newest RC
sections.content:
Drizzle ORM and Kit are free and open source. It bills you in dependency risk instead.

- **Newest release, not stable 1.0:** as of 10 November 2026, it is 1.0.0-rc.5.
- 1.0.0-rc.5 shipped 21 October 2026, and its notes list a dozen-plus BREAKING changes, from postgres-js parsers to `withReplicas` default routing and the `sqlite-proxy` rework.
- **No Studio source.** ORM and Kit are open source; Drizzle Studio is not.
- **Employment:** In March 2026 PlanetScale hired the entire core team. Drizzle's own page: "PlanetScale is our biggest sponsor, they hired us".

That is a hire, not an acquisition, and the code stays open source. Still, the people choosing the next routing default are paid by a database company.

> Do not adopt Drizzle 1.0.0-rc.5 if production policy forbids release candidates; this does not establish the suitability of earlier releases.

sections.title: Prisma bundle size, warm queries and cold starts measure different things
sections.content:
> Prisma claims 90% smaller output and 3x faster queries, from a Rust engine of roughly 14 MB (7 MB gzipped) to a compiler of about 1.6 MB (600 KB gzipped). Alex Georgiev's test, published 6 November 2026, ran two identical SQLite projects on one local machine. One developer, not a lab. For Prisma 6.19.3 versus 7.10.1 respectively, process start to first query was ~69 ms versus ~236 ms, while `node_modules` was 254.1 MiB versus 333.3 MiB.

| Measure | Prisma 6.19.3 | Prisma 7.10.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Warm `findUnique`, 2,000 sequential calls | ~0.60 ms each | ~0.19 ms each |
| Process start to first query | ~69 ms | ~236 ms |
| `node_modules` | 254.1 MiB | 333.3 MiB |

The warm row backs the vendor: 0.60 ÷ 0.19 ≈ 3.1x. The cold row runs the other way, mostly in `import` and `$connect()`.

- Cold-start ratio: 236 ÷ 69 ≈ 3.4x.
- Directory growth: (333.3 − 254.1) ÷ 254.1 × 100 ≈ 31%.

Bundle output is not directory size; warm queries are not cold starts. This informs a Prisma upgrade, not a winner over Drizzle.

sections.title: Prisma Postgres Starter crosses Pro at 5.875M operations
sections.content:
Prisma Postgres bills each query as an operation and charges separately for storage overage, but has no per-seat charge.

| Plan | Base | Included | Overage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Starter | $10 | 1M ops | $8 per million |
| Pro | $49 | 10M ops | $2 per million |
| Business | $129 | 50M ops | $1 per million |

> With n in millions of monthly operations, $10 + $8(n - 1) = $49 gives n = 5.875, or 5.875M operations. Above that, Pro is cheaper on operation charges; its $49 base covers 10M, then each million costs $2.

At 20M operations, Starter costs $10 + 19 × $8 = $162 and Pro costs $49 + 10 × $2 = $69. That $93 monthly gap comes from moving one plan up, not from new infrastructure.

- Difference: $162 − $69 = $93/month.

One line item is retiring: the Accelerate cache ends 1 December 2026. If it absorbed your reads, redo the crossover with the uncached query count.

sections.title: Drizzle's tools are free; database and runtime set the bill
sections.content:
Drizzle charges $0 for the ORM, Kit, Studio for local development and Gateway. Your chosen database and runtime set the infrastructure bill, not the maintainers' employer; Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute are optional paid services beside free Prisma ORM.

- Pick **Drizzle** if no client codegen matters and you accept the named RC's compatibility risk.
- Pick **Prisma** if generated-client workflow fits; its ORM does not require Prisma Postgres.

Check before your next deploy:

- If using Prisma Postgres, compare Starter and Pro operation charges, then add storage overage.
- Time process start to first query on your own target before trusting either Prisma figure.
- Before adopting Drizzle 1.0.0-rc.5, check its breaking changes against your application.

Pick Prisma if the generator is fine and you may want Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute on the same bill, where the operation meter meets Pro at 5.875M queries; neither ORM will ever appear on an invoice.
migration_guide: Prisma to Drizzle rewrites the data layer: every model becomes a table definition, the `prisma migrate` history becomes drizzle-kit migrations, and there is no client to generate. Drizzle to Prisma means writing one schema file that becomes the truth again, and deciding whether the generated client is committed or ignored. In both directions, the migration tooling writes SQL you review — neither one replays the other's history.

faqs.q: Do I have to use Prisma Postgres to use Prisma ORM?
faqs.a: No: the ORM is free on every plan and works without Prisma Postgres. If you do try the database, its Free plan includes 200,000 operations with the spend limit fixed at $0 and no card.

faqs.q: Can I shrink the Prisma 7 query compiler?
faqs.a: Since 7.3.0 the generator accepts `compilerBuild = "fast" | "small"`, with `fast` as the default. In Alex Georgiev's listing the SQLite compiler is 4,406,183 bytes in the fast build and 2,214,935 bytes in the small one.

faqs.q: Will long-running queries survive Prisma Postgres connection pooling?
faqs.a: Pooled connections run in transaction mode with a 10-minute query duration limit and a 60-minute idle timeout. Pooled connection caps are 10, 100, 500 and 1,000 from Free to Business, with 10, 10, 50 and 100 direct connections.

faqs.q: Which databases can Drizzle talk to?
faqs.a: Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, SingleStore, MSSQL and CockroachDB, through the standard drivers. Drizzle states the ORM has "exactly 0 dependencies".

> **Podman:** the runtime has no daemon; the desktop uses Apache License 2.0.

- Podman 6.1.4 and Podman Desktop 1.30.5 use Apache License 2.0 with no paid tier.

> Choose paid Docker Desktop for its plan controls; choose Podman when eliminating licence fees justifies Docker-only API rewrites and socket-security responsibility.

sections.title: Who should not pick Podman: teams without socket ownership
sections.content:
Podman's licence bill is $0. Its `podman system service` provides Docker v1.40 compatibility beside the native Libpod API. Socket-activated by systemd, it exits after 5 idle seconds by default.

With a rootless API service already listening:

```bash
export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock
```

Check required API calls and rewrite Docker-only handlers. The command is unavailable directly on macOS or Windows; `--time 0` disables inactivity timeout.

The man page warns:

> "the API grants full access to all Podman functionality, and thus allows arbitrary code execution as the user running the API, with no ability to limit or audit this access"

Rootless narrows whose account is exposed; it does not make the socket safe to share.

- Skip Podman if required API calls are unsupported or nobody owns socket permissions.
- Avoid TCP exposure without mutual TLS; the man page suggests SSH forwarding instead.

sections.title: Who should not pick Docker: government expecting free Desktop
sections.content:
Podman Desktop is free, Apache 2.0 and, in its own words, "trusted as part of the CNCF". It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows. Red Hat sells enterprise support as a build, the Red Hat Build of Podman Desktop, not as a licence tier.

- Docker Business includes SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, plus Hardened Docker Desktop and Image Access Management.
- Podman Desktop's enterprise path is that Red Hat build: support and long-term maintenance, not a licence tier.

Skip Docker if you are a government entity counting on the free tier; it never applied.
